title: Genetics and Inheritance
summary: How genes cause disease and how inheritance patterns are recognized.

lessons.title: DNA, Genes and Mutations

levels.kid:
Inside almost every cell in your body is a tiny instruction book called DNA. It is written with just four letters: A, T, C and G. A gene is one recipe in that book. One recipe might tell the cell how to make a protein that carries oxygen, and another tells it how to make hair color.

Your body copies this book every time a cell splits in two. Usually the copy is perfect. Sometimes a letter gets swapped, lost, or added. That change is called a mutation. Many mutations do nothing at all, like a typo in a word nobody reads. Some change a recipe so the protein does not work well, and that can cause a disease. Doctors can read these letters to find out what went wrong.
levels.hs:
DNA is a double helix: two strands twisted together, held by base pairs. Adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T), and guanine (G) pairs with cytosine (C). A gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for a product, usually a protein. Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes spread across 23 pairs of chromosomes.

The path from gene to protein is called the central dogma: DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA) in the nucleus, then the mRNA is translated into a chain of amino acids at the ribosome. Every three letters of mRNA (a codon) stands for one amino acid, and special stop codons end the chain.

A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. Types include:
- **Point mutations**: one letter changed.
- **Insertions and deletions**: letters added or removed. If the number is not a multiple of three, the reading frame shifts and everything after is garbled (a frameshift).
- **Larger changes**: whole chunks or chromosomes duplicated or lost.

Mutations can be inherited from a parent (germline) or happen in one body cell during life (somatic). Cancer is mostly driven by somatic mutations.
levels.college:
Point mutations are classified by their effect on the codon. A **silent** (synonymous) mutation changes the codon but not the amino acid, thanks to the redundancy of the genetic code. A **missense** mutation swaps one amino acid for another; sickle cell disease is the classic example (HBB Glu6Val, glutamic acid to valine at position 6 of beta-globin), which makes deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerize. A **nonsense** mutation creates a premature stop codon; the mRNA is often destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay, so little or no protein is made.

Frameshifts (insertions or deletions not divisible by three) usually produce a premature stop downstream. In-frame deletions remove amino acids but keep the frame; the most common cystic fibrosis allele, F508del, deletes three bases and removes one phenylalanine, causing CFTR misfolding.

**Trinucleotide repeat expansions** are a special class: Huntington disease (CAG), fragile X (CGG), myotonic dystrophy (CTG) and Friedreich ataxia (GAA). Many show **anticipation**, earlier onset or greater severity in later generations as the repeat grows.

Mutations also hit non-coding DNA: splice-site variants cause exon skipping, and promoter variants change how much product is made. Functionally, a variant can cause **loss of function** (the usual mechanism in recessive disease), **gain of function**, or a **dominant-negative** effect, where an abnormal protein poisons the normal one (classic in collagen disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta).

Sources of mutation include replication errors that escape proofreading and mismatch repair, spontaneous deamination, UV light (thymine dimers, repaired by nucleotide excision repair), ionizing radiation (double-strand breaks) and chemical mutagens.
levels.phd:
The modern view of a 'gene' is messier than the textbook unit. Alternative splicing lets one locus encode many isoforms; overlapping and antisense transcripts are common; and most disease-associated variants from genome-wide association studies sit in non-coding regulatory elements such as enhancers, which can act over hundreds of kilobases through chromatin looping. Disrupting the boundaries of topologically associating domains can rewire enhancer-promoter contacts and cause limb malformations without touching a coding exon.

Genotype-phenotype relationships are shaped by several layers:
- **Penetrance and expressivity**: the same variant may cause no disease in one carrier and severe disease in another, because of modifier genes, environment and chance.
- **Mosaicism**: a post-zygotic mutation is present in only some cells. Somatic mosaic activating variants in PIK3CA cause overgrowth syndromes, and mosaic GNAQ variants cause Sturge-Weber syndrome, a classic neurocutaneous disorder.
- **Haploinsufficiency vs dosage sensitivity**: for some genes one working copy is not enough; for others, an extra copy is harmful (PMP22 duplication causes Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A, while its deletion causes a different neuropathy).

Repeat expansions have unusual mechanisms beyond simple loss of function: toxic RNA gains of function (myotonic dystrophy RNA sequesters splicing regulators), repeat-associated non-AUG translation producing toxic peptides (the C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat in ALS/frontotemporal dementia), and somatic repeat instability in neurons, which genetic studies now link to the age of onset in Huntington disease.

Finally, de novo mutation rate rises with paternal age, because sperm precursors keep dividing throughout life. This is one reason de novo variants dominate the genetics of severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathies.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, the question is rarely 'is there a mutation?' and more often 'does this variant explain this patient?' A few habits separate good clinicians here.

First, think about mechanism before ordering. A suspected repeat disorder (Huntington, fragile X, myotonic dystrophy, Friedreich ataxia, many spinocerebellar ataxias) needs a targeted repeat test, because standard short-read exome sequencing can miss or mis-size expansions. A patient with a large deletion may be missed by a test designed to find single-letter changes.

Second, remember somatic vs germline. A tumor sequencing report may list variants that are also in the patient's blood, which changes counseling for the whole family. In neurosurgery this matters directly: a young patient with multiple schwannomas or meningiomas suggests NF2-related schwannomatosis, and a child with a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma raises tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2), which in turn changes surveillance and medical options such as mTOR inhibitors.

Third, anticipation and parental age are history clues. A family where a disease appears earlier each generation points toward a repeat expansion; in Huntington disease, juvenile onset is more often seen with paternal transmission because the CAG repeat tends to expand in the male germline.

Fourth, mosaicism explains odd presentations: segmental findings, a parent with a milder form, or recurrence in siblings despite 'de novo' results in the first child (gonadal mosaicism). Counsel families that recurrence risk after a de novo finding is low but not zero.

Finally, a classic pitfall: equating a variant in a disease gene with a diagnosis. Many people carry rare variants in disease genes with no consequence. The phenotype has to fit the gene, and the mechanism has to fit the variant.

keyPoints: Gene → mRNA (transcription) → protein (translation); codons are 3 bases
Point mutations: silent, missense (sickle cell HBB Glu6Val), nonsense (premature stop)
Indels not divisible by 3 cause frameshifts; CF F508del is an in-frame deletion
Repeat expansions (Huntington CAG, fragile X CGG) can show anticipation
Germline mutations are inherited; somatic mutations arise in one cell line (most cancer)
Mechanisms: loss of function, gain of function, dominant-negative

examples.tr: A missense mutation in HBB swaps glutamic acid for valine, so deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerizes and red cells sickle.
An expanded CAG repeat in HTT; longer repeats tend to mean earlier onset.

test.q: Which base pairs with adenine in DNA?
test.explain: In DNA, A pairs with T and G pairs with C. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, not DNA.

test.q: The process of copying DNA into mRNA is called:
test.explain: Transcription makes mRNA from DNA in the nucleus; translation makes protein from mRNA at the ribosome.

test.q: A mutation changes a codon but the same amino acid is still made. This is a:
test.explain: The genetic code is redundant, so some codon changes do not change the amino acid.

test.q: Sickle cell disease is caused by which type of mutation in HBB?
test.explain: One base change swaps glutamic acid for valine at position 6 of beta-globin.

test.q: Deleting 2 bases from a coding sequence usually causes:
choices: A nonsense codon at the deletion site
test.explain: Two is not a multiple of three, so every codon downstream is read in the wrong frame.

test.q: Which disease is caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion?
test.explain: HTT CAG expansion causes Huntington disease. CF and sickle cell are not repeat disorders.

test.q: A mutation that arises in one body cell during life and is not passed to children is:
test.explain: Somatic mutations stay in that cell's descendants; germline mutations are in eggs or sperm and can be inherited.

test.q: An abnormal protein that interferes with the normal copy's function is called a:
test.explain: Classic in collagen disorders: mutant chains get built into the triple helix and spoil it.

test.q: A mutation that creates a premature stop codon is a ___ mutation.
test.explain: Nonsense = 'no sense': the protein is cut short, and the mRNA is often destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay.

test.q: What term describes earlier onset of a disease in each new generation?
test.explain: Seen in repeat expansion disorders, because the repeat tends to grow when passed on.

test.q: The most common cystic fibrosis allele, F508del, removes one ___ from CFTR.
test.explain: F is the code for phenylalanine; the deletion of 3 bases removes it without shifting the frame.

test.q: Three bases of mRNA that code for one amino acid are called a what?
test.explain: Codons are read in triplets by the ribosome; three of them are stop codons.

kidTest.q: What is DNA like?
choices: A special type of bone in your back
A kind of food that gives you energy
A big muscle that helps you move
An instruction book for your body
kidTest.explain: DNA holds the instructions your cells follow.

kidTest.q: How many letters does the DNA alphabet have?
kidTest.explain: Just four: A, T, C and G.

kidTest.q: A gene is like:
kidTest.explain: Each gene is one recipe, often for one protein.

kidTest.q: A mistake or change in DNA letters is called a:
kidTest.explain: A mutation is a change in the DNA letters.

kidTest.q: Do all mutations make you sick?
kidTest.explain: Lots of mutations are like typos in words nobody reads.

kidTest.q: Fill in: A, T, C and ___ are the DNA letters.
kidTest.explain: The four DNA letters are A, T, C and G.

advancedTest.q: A child has a severe epileptic encephalopathy; both parents are unaffected and exome shows a heterozygous variant absent in both parents. The most likely explanation is:
advancedTest.explain: De novo heterozygous variants are a leading cause of severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Gonadal mosaicism in a parent still gives a small recurrence risk.

advancedTest.q: Why might standard short-read exome sequencing miss Huntington disease?
choices: Repeat expansions are hard to size with short reads
Huntington is caused by a silent mutation
HTT is on the Y chromosome
advancedTest.explain: Long repeats exceed the read length; a targeted repeat-sizing test is the right test.

advancedTest.q: The C9orf72 repeat expansion in ALS/FTD is thought to cause disease partly through:
choices: A Y-linked deletion that removes motor neuron survival genes
A single missense change that alters SOD1 enzyme activity
Toxic RNA and repeat-associated non-AUG translated peptides
Loss of mitochondrial DNA copies in upper motor neurons
advancedTest.explain: Proposed mechanisms include RNA foci, RAN-translated dipeptide repeat proteins and reduced C9orf72 protein.

advancedTest.q: What term describes a mutation present in only some of a person's cells?
advancedTest.explain: Mosaicism comes from a post-zygotic mutation; gonadal mosaicism explains recurrence in siblings.

lessons.title: Mendelian Inheritance Patterns

levels.kid:
You get two copies of most genes: one from your mom and one from your dad. They are like two flashlights pointing at the same spot.

Some traits are **dominant**. One copy is enough to show it, like one bright flashlight lighting the whole room. Other traits are **recessive**. You only see them when both copies are the same, like needing both flashlights to be a special color.

Some genes live on the X chromosome. Boys have only one X, so if that one X has a broken gene, there is no backup. That is why boys get some conditions, like color blindness, more often than girls.

Doctors draw family trees with squares for boys and circles for girls to see how a trait moves through a family.
levels.hs:
Gregor Mendel, experimenting with pea plants in the 1860s, showed that traits are passed on in units we now call genes. Each person has two copies (alleles) of each autosomal gene. If both are the same, you are **homozygous**; if they differ, **heterozygous**.

The main single-gene patterns:
- **Autosomal dominant**: one changed copy causes the condition. An affected parent has a 50% chance of passing it to each child. It shows up in every generation, in males and females. Example: Huntington disease.
- **Autosomal recessive**: two changed copies needed. Two healthy carrier parents have a 25% chance of an affected child with each pregnancy. It often skips generations. Examples: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease.
- **X-linked recessive**: mostly affects males, passed through carrier mothers. Fathers cannot pass it to sons, because they give sons their Y. Examples: hemophilia A, Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- **X-linked dominant**: an affected father passes it to all daughters and no sons.
- **Mitochondrial**: passed only from the mother to all her children.

Doctors record family history in a **pedigree**: squares are males, circles females, filled shapes affected, and a line through a symbol means deceased. Reading the pattern helps estimate risk for other relatives.
levels.college:
Pedigree analysis works by elimination. Clues for **autosomal dominant (AD)** inheritance: vertical transmission across generations, males and females equally affected, and male-to-male transmission (which rules out X-linked). AD disorders often involve structural proteins or receptors: Marfan syndrome (FBN1), familial hypercholesterolemia (LDLR), neurofibromatosis type 1, adult polycystic kidney disease, Huntington disease.

**Autosomal recessive (AR)**: horizontal pattern (affected siblings), unaffected parents, increased likelihood with consanguinity. AR disorders are often enzyme deficiencies, because half the enzyme activity is usually enough: phenylketonuria, Tay-Sachs, most inborn errors of metabolism. A healthy sibling of an affected child has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier, not 1/2, because the affected genotype is already excluded.

**X-linked recessive (XLR)**: affected males linked through unaffected females, no male-to-male transmission. All daughters of an affected male are obligate carriers. Carrier females may show mild signs due to skewed X-inactivation.

**X-linked dominant**: affected fathers pass it to all daughters; examples include hypophosphatemic rickets and Rett syndrome (MECP2), which is usually de novo and mainly seen in females.

Complications that blur patterns:
- **Incomplete penetrance**: carriers without disease (BRCA1/2).
- **Variable expressivity**: same variant, different severity (NF1).
- **Genetic heterogeneity**: one phenotype, many genes (locus heterogeneity) or many variants in one gene (allelic heterogeneity).
- **Pleiotropy**: one gene, many organ effects (Marfan: lens, aorta, skeleton).
- **Imprinting**: Prader-Willi (loss of paternal 15q11-13) vs Angelman (loss of maternal UBE3A).

Hardy-Weinberg: for an AR disease with frequency q², the carrier frequency is about 2q.
levels.phd:
Mendelian patterns are idealizations, and much of medical genetics lives in the exceptions.

**Penetrance** is age-dependent for many adult-onset AD disorders; a 30-year-old unaffected child of a Huntington patient is still at substantial risk. For Huntington, repeat length itself defines penetrance bands: 40 or more CAG repeats is fully penetrant, 36 to 39 reduced penetrance, and 27 to 35 an intermediate range that does not cause disease but may expand in the next generation.

**Imprinting** means the parental origin of an allele matters. In Prader-Willi syndrome, paternally expressed genes at 15q11-q13 are lost (by paternal deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, or an imprinting defect). In Angelman syndrome, the maternally expressed UBE3A is lost in neurons. Uniparental disomy can also unmask recessive disease when a carrier parent's chromosome is duplicated.

**Mitochondrial disease** shows heteroplasmy: a cell holds a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA, and the mutant fraction varies between tissues and children because of the mitochondrial bottleneck in oocytes. A threshold effect means symptoms appear only above a certain mutant load. Many 'mitochondrial' diseases are actually caused by nuclear genes and follow Mendelian rules.

**Digenic and oligogenic inheritance**, modifier genes, and polygenic background mean the line between Mendelian and complex disease is a spectrum. Polygenic risk scores can shift the penetrance of a monogenic variant; for example, the breast cancer risk in BRCA carriers varies with polygenic background.

X-inactivation adds noise for females: random lyonization creates mosaic tissues, and skewing can produce a manifesting carrier of Duchenne or Fabry disease. Fabry is a good reminder that 'X-linked recessive' is a historical label; many heterozygous women have clinically significant disease.
levels.expert:
Taking a three-generation family history is still one of the highest-yield, cheapest tests in medicine, and it is often done badly. A few practical rules:

Ask specifically. 'Any family history?' gets 'no.' Ask about early deaths, sudden deaths under 50, early heart attacks, cancers and the age at diagnosis, miscarriages, consanguinity, learning disability, seizures, and anyone with 'the same thing.' Ask about ancestry, because carrier frequencies differ between populations.

Draw it. A quick pedigree on the note reveals patterns faster than prose, and it lets you spot male-to-male transmission, which kills an X-linked hypothesis.

Think about apparent sporadic cases. Small families, early deaths from other causes, adoption, misattributed parentage, incomplete penetrance, and de novo variants all make a dominant condition look sporadic. NF1 is a good example: roughly half of cases are de novo, yet the patient's children have a 50% risk.

Use inheritance to drive care. Familial hypercholesterolemia identified in one patient should trigger cascade testing of relatives. A patient with a cerebral aneurysm and a first-degree relative with aneurysm or polycystic kidney disease deserves screening thinking; ADPKD is a known risk factor for intracranial aneurysms, which is directly relevant in neurosurgery. Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (AD) can present with brain or spinal arteriovenous malformations.

Risk numbers must be framed carefully. '25% each pregnancy' does not mean one in four children; each pregnancy is independent. Avoid blame language; carriers did nothing wrong.

Know when to hand off. Complex counseling, predictive testing for untreatable adult-onset disease like Huntington, and reproductive options belong with genetic counselors, who follow protocols that include pre-test counseling and the right not to know.

keyPoints: AD: every generation, 50% risk to each child, male-to-male transmission possible
AR: carrier parents, 25% risk per pregnancy, often enzyme defects, linked to consanguinity
XLR: affects males via carrier mothers, never father to son
Mitochondrial: mother passes to all children; heteroplasmy causes variable severity
Penetrance, expressivity, imprinting and de novo variants blur classic patterns
Pedigree: square = male, circle = female, filled = affected

examples.src: Healthy sibling of a child with cystic fibrosis
examples.tr: Has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier, because the affected genotype is excluded.
All his daughters are carriers; none of his sons are affected (they get his Y).

test.q: Two carrier parents for an autosomal recessive disease. Chance each child is affected?
test.explain: Each parent passes the variant with probability 1/2, so 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

test.q: An affected parent with an autosomal dominant condition. Chance each child inherits it?
test.explain: The affected parent has one changed copy and passes either copy with equal chance.

test.q: Which finding rules out X-linked inheritance in a pedigree?
test.explain: A father gives his son his Y chromosome, not his X.

test.q: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited as:
test.explain: DMD (dystrophin) is on the X chromosome; mostly boys are affected, via carrier mothers.

test.q: A mitochondrial disease is passed:
choices: From the father to sons only
From the mother to all her children
test.explain: Mitochondria in the embryo come from the egg.

test.q: A healthy sibling of a child with an autosomal recessive disease has what chance of being a carrier?
test.explain: Of the 3 unaffected possibilities (AA, Aa, aA), 2 are carriers.

test.q: Same variant, but family members have very different severity. This is:
test.explain: Expressivity describes how severely a variant shows; penetrance is whether it shows at all.

test.q: Marfan syndrome affects eye lens, aorta and skeleton. One gene affecting many organs is:
test.explain: FBN1 (fibrillin-1) is used in connective tissue throughout the body.

test.q: Which type of disorder is most often autosomal recessive?
test.explain: Half the enzyme activity is usually enough, so carriers are healthy and disease needs two hits.

test.q: In a pedigree, what shape represents a male?
test.explain: Squares are males, circles are females; filled means affected.

test.q: A person with two different alleles of a gene is ___.
test.explain: Two identical alleles = homozygous; two different = heterozygous.

test.q: Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome both involve chromosome 15 and which phenomenon where parental origin matters?
test.explain: Genomic imprinting: some genes are expressed only from one parent's copy.

kidTest.q: How many copies of most genes do you have?
kidTest.explain: One copy from mom and one from dad.

kidTest.q: A dominant trait needs how many copies to show?
kidTest.explain: One copy is enough, like one bright flashlight.

kidTest.q: A recessive trait shows when you have:
kidTest.explain: Recessive traits need both copies.

kidTest.q: On a family tree, a circle means:
kidTest.explain: Circles are females and squares are males.

kidTest.q: Why do boys get color blindness more often?
kidTest.explain: With one X there is no backup copy.

kidTest.q: You get one copy of a gene from your mom and one from your ___.
kidTest.explain: Each parent gives one copy.

advancedTest.q: A 30-year-old with 38 CAG repeats in HTT and no symptoms. Best description?
choices: Full penetrance; certain to develop disease by 40
Reduced-penetrance range; may or may not develop disease
Intermediate allele with no personal risk
advancedTest.explain: 36-39 repeats is reduced penetrance; 40+ is full penetrance; 27-35 is intermediate (no disease but may expand).

advancedTest.q: A child has Prader-Willi syndrome with no deletion found. Which mechanism is most likely?
advancedTest.explain: PWS = loss of paternally expressed genes; two maternal copies (maternal UPD) is the second most common cause.

advancedTest.q: A woman heterozygous for a Fabry disease (GLA) variant has cardiac and kidney involvement. Best explanation?
choices: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy distributing mutant DNA unevenly
Fabry disease is autosomal dominant, so one copy is enough
X-inactivation leaves many cells expressing only the mutant allele
She must carry two mutant copies, one from each parent
advancedTest.explain: Random or skewed lyonization makes heterozygous females mosaics; many Fabry heterozygotes have real disease.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a ruptured cerebral aneurysm has a father on dialysis for kidney cysts. Which inherited condition should you think of?
choices: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked disorder
Cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder
Fragile X syndrome, a CGG repeat expansion disorder
advancedTest.explain: ADPKD is associated with intracranial aneurysms; first-degree relatives may warrant screening discussion.

lessons.title: Chromosomal Disorders

levels.kid:
Your DNA is packed into 46 little bundles called chromosomes. They come in 23 pairs, like 23 pairs of socks in a drawer. One sock of each pair came from mom and one from dad.

Sometimes a person has an extra chromosome, or one is missing, or a piece breaks off. That is a lot of instructions changed at once, so it can change how the body and brain grow.

The most well-known example is Down syndrome. People with Down syndrome have three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two. They can go to school, have jobs, make friends and live full lives, and doctors help with things like heart checks.

Doctors can count chromosomes by looking at them under a microscope, a picture called a karyotype.
levels.hs:
Humans normally have 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes plus two sex chromosomes (XX or XY). A **karyotype** is a picture of all of them, arranged in pairs.

The biggest group of chromosomal disorders is **aneuploidy**, the wrong number of chromosomes. It usually comes from **nondisjunction**, when chromosomes fail to separate properly while eggs or sperm are made. The risk rises with the mother's age.
- **Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)**: intellectual disability, characteristic facial features, heart defects, and a higher risk of early Alzheimer disease.
- **Trisomy 18 (Edwards)** and **trisomy 13 (Patau)**: severe, with major birth defects; most babies do not survive the first year.
- **Turner syndrome (45,X)**: females with short stature, ovarian failure, and some heart defects.
- **Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)**: males who are often tall, with small testes and infertility.

Other changes involve pieces of chromosomes: **deletions** (a piece missing), **duplications**, and **translocations** (pieces swapped between chromosomes). A small deletion on chromosome 22 causes 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, which affects the heart, immune system and palate.

Most trisomies of other chromosomes cause miscarriage; aneuploidy is a major cause of early pregnancy loss.
levels.college:
**Nondisjunction** can happen in meiosis I (homologs fail to separate) or meiosis II (sister chromatids fail to separate); most trisomy 21 arises in maternal meiosis I, and risk climbs steeply with maternal age. About 95% of Down syndrome is free trisomy 21; a few percent arise from a **Robertsonian translocation** (often 14;21), which matters because a balanced carrier parent has a substantial recurrence risk; the remainder are mosaic.

Robertsonian translocations fuse two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) at the centromere. **Reciprocal translocations** swap segments between non-homologous chromosomes. Balanced carriers are usually healthy but have recurrent miscarriage or children with unbalanced karyotypes. The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22), creating BCR-ABL1, is the famous somatic translocation in chronic myeloid leukemia.

Key syndromes:
- **Trisomy 21**: hypotonia, single palmar crease, AV septal defect, duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, hypothyroidism, leukemia risk, atlantoaxial instability, early-onset Alzheimer (APP is on chromosome 21).
- **Trisomy 18**: clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia.
- **Trisomy 13**: holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly.
- **Turner (45,X)**: lymphedema at birth, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, streak ovaries, normal intelligence usually.
- **Klinefelter (47,XXY)**: hypogonadism with high gonadotropins, gynecomastia, infertility.

**Microdeletion syndromes** are too small for a standard karyotype: 22q11.2 deletion (conotruncal heart defects, thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia, psychiatric risk), Williams syndrome (7q11.23; elastin; supravalvular aortic stenosis; very social personality), and Cri-du-chat (5p deletion).

Sex chromosome aneuploidies are generally milder than autosomal ones, because of X-inactivation and the small number of genes on Y.
levels.phd:
Why are some aneuploidies viable and most not? Chromosome 21 is the smallest human autosome, carrying a few hundred protein-coding genes; 13 and 18 are also relatively gene-poor. Phenotype is thought to result from gene dosage imbalance: a 1.5-fold increase in many genes, plus secondary disturbances in genome-wide expression. Specific genes on 21 have been linked to features, for example extra APP to the near-universal Alzheimer neuropathology by middle age, and DYRK1A to neurodevelopmental effects, though no single 'Down syndrome critical region' explains everything.

Maternal age effect: oocytes arrest in prophase I from fetal life until ovulation, sometimes for four decades. Gradual loss of cohesin holding sister chromatids together, and weakening checkpoints, are leading explanations for rising nondisjunction.

Mosaicism can arise by post-zygotic nondisjunction or by **trisomy rescue**, where a trisomic zygote loses one copy. If both remaining copies came from the same parent, the result is uniparental disomy, linking aneuploidy to imprinting disorders such as Prader-Willi. **Confined placental mosaicism** explains discordant prenatal screening results, where cell-free DNA (largely placental) shows aneuploidy that the fetus lacks.

Copy number variants (CNVs) bridge chromosomal and single-gene disorders. Low-copy repeats flanking regions like 22q11.2, 7q11.23 and 15q11-q13 promote non-allelic homologous recombination, explaining recurrent deletions of identical size. Recurrent CNVs at 16p11.2, 15q13.3 and 1q21.1 show incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity for autism, epilepsy, intellectual disability and schizophrenia, illustrating that dosage-sensitive regions act as risk factors rather than deterministic causes.
levels.expert:
Clinicians meet chromosomal disorders in two ways: as known diagnoses that change management, and as hidden diagnoses waiting to be found.

Known diagnoses carry standard surveillance. In Down syndrome: echocardiogram at diagnosis, regular thyroid testing, hearing and vision checks, screening for sleep apnea, celiac awareness, and attention to neck symptoms. Atlantoaxial instability is a real anesthesia and neurosurgical concern: avoid aggressive neck manipulation during intubation and positioning, and take new gait change, neck pain, or bowel or bladder change seriously as possible cord compression. Adults with Down syndrome develop Alzheimer disease decades earlier than the general population; new seizures in a middle-aged adult with Down syndrome often signal it.

In Turner syndrome, look for coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve, and keep aortic dissection in mind. In 22q11.2 deletion, check calcium (hypocalcemic seizures can be the presenting event), immune function, and watch for later psychiatric illness.

Hidden diagnoses: a child with developmental delay, autism or multiple anomalies should have chromosomal microarray as a first-tier test; it detects CNVs far below karyotype resolution. A karyotype is still needed for balanced translocations, which microarray cannot see, so recurrent miscarriage in a couple calls for parental karyotypes.

Two pitfalls. First, prenatal cell-free DNA screening is a screen: a positive result needs diagnostic confirmation by CVS or amniocentesis, because of false positives, confined placental mosaicism, or even an undiagnosed maternal condition. Second, mosaic karyotypes can be missed if few cells are counted, and a normal blood karyotype does not exclude tissue mosaicism, for example in skin.

Language matters: say 'a child with Down syndrome', and present the diagnosis with real information about quality of life, not just a list of problems.

keyPoints: Normal karyotype: 46,XX or 46,XY; aneuploidy = wrong number, usually from nondisjunction
Trisomy 21 (Down), 18 (Edwards), 13 (Patau); risk rises with maternal age
Turner 45,X and Klinefelter 47,XXY are sex chromosome aneuploidies
Robertsonian translocations (e.g. 14;21) cause familial Down syndrome
Microdeletions (22q11.2, Williams 7q11.23) need microarray or FISH, not a standard karyotype
Microarray detects CNVs but not balanced translocations

examples.src: Newborn with hypotonia, AV septal defect and duodenal atresia
examples.tr: Classic trisomy 21 constellation; confirm with karyotype.

examples.src: Infant with hypocalcemic seizure and a conotruncal heart defect

test.q: How many chromosomes does a typical human cell have?
test.explain: 23 pairs = 46: 22 pairs of autosomes plus XX or XY.

test.q: Failure of chromosomes to separate during meiosis is called:
test.explain: Nondisjunction gives gametes with an extra or missing chromosome.

test.q: Down syndrome is most often caused by:
choices: A Robertsonian translocation in most cases
test.explain: About 95% is free trisomy 21, mostly maternal meiosis I; translocation and mosaic forms are less common.

test.q: Which karyotype is Turner syndrome?
test.explain: Turner = one X only; females with short stature and ovarian failure.

test.q: Klinefelter syndrome is:
test.explain: An extra X in a male: tall, small testes, infertility, high gonadotropins.

test.q: Holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and extra fingers in a newborn suggest:
test.explain: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) classically shows midline brain and face defects plus polydactyly.

test.q: Which cardiac lesion is classic for Turner syndrome?
test.explain: Coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve are typical of Turner.

test.q: Hypocalcemia, thymic hypoplasia and a conotruncal heart defect suggest:
test.explain: The 22q11.2 deletion disrupts third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development.

test.q: Which test is first-tier for a child with unexplained developmental delay?
test.explain: Microarray detects small copy number changes a karyotype cannot see.

test.q: Why adults with Down syndrome get early Alzheimer disease: the ___ gene is on chromosome 21.
test.explain: Three copies of amyloid precursor protein mean more amyloid-beta.

test.q: A picture of a person's chromosomes arranged in pairs is called a what?
test.explain: Karyotypes count chromosomes and show large structural changes.

test.q: The Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukemia is a translocation between chromosomes 9 and ___.
test.explain: t(9;22) creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene.

kidTest.q: What are chromosomes?
kidTest.explain: DNA is packed into chromosomes.

kidTest.q: How many chromosomes do most people have?
kidTest.explain: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.

kidTest.q: People with Down syndrome have three copies of chromosome:
kidTest.explain: That's why it's also called trisomy 21.

kidTest.q: Can people with Down syndrome go to school and have friends?
kidTest.explain: They can live full lives with the right support.

kidTest.q: A picture of all the chromosomes is called a:
kidTest.explain: Doctors use a karyotype to count chromosomes.

kidTest.q: Chromosomes come in 23 ___.
kidTest.explain: Like pairs of socks: one from mom, one from dad.

advancedTest.q: A couple has a child with Down syndrome due to a Robertsonian 14;21 translocation. What is the next step?
choices: No testing; recurrence risk is the same as the population
advancedTest.explain: A parent may be a balanced carrier, which greatly raises recurrence risk compared with free trisomy.

advancedTest.q: Cell-free DNA screening shows trisomy 13, but amniocentesis is normal. Most likely explanation?
choices: A sample mix-up at the laboratory
advancedTest.explain: cfDNA comes mostly from the placenta, which can carry an aneuploidy the fetus lacks.

advancedTest.q: A child with Down syndrome develops new neck pain, gait change and urinary incontinence. Priority concern?
choices: Celiac disease causing malabsorption and neuropathy
Early-onset Alzheimer disease with gait apraxia
Hypothyroidism causing myopathy and slowed gait
advancedTest.explain: Ligament laxity at C1-C2 can compress the cord; urgent imaging and neurosurgical input.

advancedTest.q: Why can't chromosomal microarray detect a balanced reciprocal translocation?
choices: The breakpoints are always in introns
No DNA is gained or lost
Microarray only reads the X chromosome
advancedTest.explain: Microarray measures copy number; a balanced rearrangement has normal dosage.

lessons.title: Genetic Testing in the Clinic

levels.kid:
Doctors have special tests that can read a person's DNA, often from a little blood or spit.

Some tests look at the whole bundle of chromosomes, like counting books on a shelf. Other tests read the letters inside one gene, like reading one page very carefully. Some read almost all the recipes at once.

Every new baby gets a tiny heel poke so doctors can test for some rare problems early. Finding them early means doctors can help right away, sometimes just by changing what the baby eats.

Genetic tests can be confusing, so there are special helpers called genetic counselors. They explain what the results mean and help families decide what to do next.
levels.hs:
Genetic tests answer different questions, so choosing the right one matters.
- **Karyotype**: counts chromosomes and shows big rearrangements.
- **FISH**: glowing probes that stick to one specific chromosome region, good for checking a suspected deletion.
- **Chromosomal microarray**: finds small missing or extra pieces (copy number variants) across the genome.
- **Single-gene or panel tests**: read genes linked to a specific condition, such as a panel for inherited heart muscle disease.
- **Exome sequencing**: reads the protein-coding parts of about 20,000 genes. **Genome sequencing** reads almost everything.

**Newborn screening** uses a few drops of blood from a heel prick to check for treatable conditions such as phenylketonuria (PKU), congenital hypothyroidism and sickle cell disease. Babies with PKU can avoid brain damage with a special diet started early.

Results are not always simple. A test can be **positive** (a disease-causing variant), **negative**, or show a **variant of uncertain significance (VUS)**, which means nobody yet knows if it matters. A VUS should not be treated as a diagnosis.

Genetic testing raises ethical questions: privacy, insurance, and results that affect relatives who never asked to be tested. That is why **genetic counseling** before and after testing is standard.
levels.college:
Choosing a test starts with the suspected mechanism:
- **Aneuploidy or large rearrangement** → karyotype (plus FISH for rapid targeted answers).
- **Copy number variants** → chromosomal microarray (first-tier for developmental delay, autism, multiple anomalies).
- **Single-nucleotide variants and small indels** → gene panel, exome or genome sequencing.
- **Repeat expansions** → targeted repeat assay (PCR plus Southern blot or repeat-primed PCR).
- **Imprinting disorders** → methylation testing.
- **Mitochondrial DNA variants** → mtDNA sequencing, ideally in an affected tissue such as muscle.

Next-generation sequencing generates millions of short reads aligned to a reference genome. Variants are classified with the ACMG/AMP framework into five tiers: **pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign, benign**. Evidence includes population frequency (common variants are rarely causative for rare disease), computational predictions, functional studies, segregation in the family, and whether the variant is de novo.

**Trio sequencing** (patient plus both parents) speeds interpretation by spotting de novo variants and phasing compound heterozygotes. **Secondary findings**: labs may report pathogenic variants in a defined list of actionable genes (such as BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome genes, LDLR) unrelated to the original question, if the patient consented.

**Pharmacogenomics** applies genetics to drug response: HLA-B*57:01 testing before abacavir prevents hypersensitivity, HLA-B*15:02 predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome in some Asian ancestries, and CYP2C19 variants affect clopidogrel activation.

In the US, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA, 2008) bars genetic discrimination in health insurance and employment, but not in life, disability or long-term care insurance.
levels.phd:
Diagnostic yield tells the story of the field. Microarray diagnoses roughly 15-20% of children with unexplained developmental delay or multiple anomalies; exome sequencing roughly 25-40% in similar cohorts, higher in critically ill infants. Genome sequencing adds structural variants, deep intronic splice variants and some repeats, and long-read technologies now resolve repeat expansions, phase haplotypes and read through regions short reads cannot map, such as segmental duplications.

A negative exome is not a negative genome. Missed diagnoses come from variants outside targeted regions, mosaic variants below detection thresholds in blood, genes not yet linked to disease, and interpretive failures. Systematic reanalysis of old exome data a few years later yields new diagnoses in a meaningful fraction of cases, as gene-disease knowledge grows.

RNA sequencing from an accessible tissue can demonstrate aberrant splicing, turning a VUS into a likely pathogenic call. Functional assays, such as saturation genome editing that tests every possible single-nucleotide change in a gene like BRCA1, increasingly provide evidence before a variant is ever seen in a patient.

Equity problems are real. Reference databases overrepresent European ancestry, so people of other ancestries receive more VUS results, and some historical 'pathogenic' calls have been reclassified once population data showed the variants were common in under-studied groups. Polygenic scores also transfer poorly across ancestries.

Cell-free DNA has created whole fields: non-invasive prenatal screening, liquid biopsy that tracks tumor DNA in blood, and, in neuro-oncology, cerebrospinal fluid tumor DNA for brain tumors that shed little into blood.
levels.expert:
Practical rules for ordering and acting on genetic tests.

Pick the test for the question. Ordering an exome for suspected Huntington disease or fragile X wastes time; those need repeat assays. For a child with global delay, start with microarray (and fragile X testing in many protocols), then move to exome or genome sequencing, ideally as a trio. In a critically ill newborn, rapid genome sequencing can return results in days and change management.

Pre-test counseling covers what the test can and cannot find, the chance of VUS and secondary findings, implications for relatives, and insurance issues. For predictive testing in untreatable adult-onset disease, follow established protocols; testing minors for adult-onset untreatable conditions is generally discouraged, preserving the child's right to decide later.

Never act on a VUS as if it were pathogenic. Do not remove organs, change surgery, or test relatives for a VUS outside a research or segregation context. Do recontact or recheck: classifications change.

Read the report fully: the sequencing method, coverage of the gene of interest, whether deletions were assessed, and the zygosity. A 'heterozygous pathogenic variant' in a recessive gene makes a carrier, not a diagnosis, unless a second variant is found.

In neurosurgery and neuro-oncology, molecular diagnosis is now part of the tumor name: WHO classification integrates markers like IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion and H3 K27 alteration. Germline testing matters too: multiple schwannomas suggest NF2-related schwannomatosis; hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum or spine suggest von Hippel-Lindau disease, which demands surveillance of kidneys, adrenals and eyes; and tumor findings can reveal a cancer predisposition syndrome such as Li-Fraumeni (TP53).

When in doubt, involve genetics early. They save time, money and errors.

keyPoints: Match the test to the mechanism: karyotype, FISH, microarray, sequencing, repeat assay, methylation
Variants are classed pathogenic, likely pathogenic, VUS, likely benign, benign
A VUS is not a diagnosis; do not act on it clinically
Newborn screening catches treatable conditions early (PKU, hypothyroidism, sickle cell)
Pharmacogenomics: HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir, HLA-B*15:02 and carbamazepine
Genetic counseling before and after testing is standard care

examples.src: Exome shows one pathogenic CFTR variant, patient has no other findings
examples.tr: That makes a carrier; a second variant (or deletion) is needed for a recessive diagnosis.

examples.src: Cerebellar hemangioblastoma in a young adult
examples.tr: Consider germline testing for von Hippel-Lindau disease.

test.q: Which test is best for finding small missing or extra chromosome pieces across the genome?
test.explain: Microarray detects copy number variants far below karyotype resolution.

test.q: A suspected fragile X syndrome is best tested with:
test.explain: Fragile X is a CGG repeat expansion that standard sequencing can miss.

test.q: What does 'VUS' stand for?
test.explain: A VUS might matter or might not; current evidence cannot say.

test.q: How should a VUS be used in clinical decisions?
choices: It should not be treated as a diagnosis
It means the gene is functioning fine
test.explain: Management should be based on the clinical picture, not on the VUS.

test.q: Babies with PKU found on newborn screening can avoid brain damage by:
test.explain: Restricting phenylalanine prevents toxic buildup.

test.q: Exome sequencing reads:
test.explain: The exome is the ~1-2% of the genome that codes for protein.

test.q: Sequencing a patient plus both parents is called:
test.explain: Trios help spot de novo variants and figure out which parent each variant came from.

test.q: HLA-B*57:01 testing is done before giving which drug?
test.explain: Carriers of HLA-B*57:01 are at high risk of abacavir hypersensitivity.

test.q: In the US, GINA protects against genetic discrimination in:
test.explain: GINA does not cover life, disability or long-term care insurance.

test.q: What kind of professional explains genetic test results and helps families decide?
test.explain: Genetic counselors handle pre- and post-test counseling.

test.q: Imprinting disorders like Prader-Willi syndrome are diagnosed with ___ testing.
test.explain: Methylation analysis detects deletion, UPD and imprinting defects together.

test.q: Which glowing-probe test checks one specific chromosome region?
test.explain: Fluorescence in situ hybridization uses labeled probes for a targeted region.

kidTest.q: Genetic tests can read a person's:
kidTest.explain: They read the DNA letters or count chromosomes.

kidTest.q: Doctors can get DNA for a test from:
kidTest.explain: Blood and saliva both contain cells with DNA.

kidTest.q: New babies get a tiny heel poke to:
kidTest.explain: Newborn screening catches treatable problems early.

kidTest.q: Who helps families understand genetic test results?
kidTest.explain: Genetic counselors explain what results mean.

kidTest.q: Why is finding a problem early good?
kidTest.explain: Early help can stop problems before they start.

kidTest.q: A baby's heel poke test is called newborn ___.
kidTest.explain: Newborn screening checks every baby.

advancedTest.q: Exome sequencing in a child with ataxia is negative. Which is NOT a common reason an exome misses the diagnosis?
choices: The child's chromosome count is normal
advancedTest.explain: A normal chromosome count has nothing to do with exome sensitivity; the others are classic exome blind spots.

advancedTest.q: Why do people of non-European ancestry receive more VUS results?
choices: Their genomes carry many more pathogenic mutations
Exome sequencing chemistry reads their DNA poorly
Labs apply stricter classification rules for them
advancedTest.explain: Without population frequency data, rare-looking but common variants stay uncertain.

advancedTest.q: A cerebellar hemangioblastoma is found in a 25-year-old. Which surveillance is most relevant if VHL is confirmed?
advancedTest.explain: VHL causes renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and retinal hemangioblastomas.

advancedTest.q: Testing a healthy 10-year-old for a Huntington variant at the parents' request is generally:
choices: Recommended, so the family can plan schooling and careers early
Done routinely as part of newborn screening in most states
Required by law when one parent carries the expanded allele
Discouraged; preserve the child's right to decide as an adult
advancedTest.explain: Predictive testing for untreatable adult-onset conditions is usually deferred until the person can consent.
